input: Design an A/B test for changing our checkout button from 'Continue' to 'Pay now'. Checkout conversion is 3.1% on about 40,000 sessions a week.
expected_outcome: Uses the A/B test design structure: a falsifiable hypothesis with the expected direction and reason, one primary metric (checkout conversion), secondary and guardrail metrics (refunds, support contacts, AOV), a sample size and duration derived from the stated baseline and a stated minimum detectable effect, control and variant definitions, early-stop rules, a significance threshold, and decision criteria written before launch.

input: Write a spec for an AI agent that triages our inbound sales leads.
expected_outcome: Does not jump straight to a finished spec: asks the grouped interview questions first (job and scope, who is affected, worst realistic wrong action, which systems it reads and writes, whose credentials, sensitive data, which actions may run with no human, approvers and timeouts, how it will be tested, who signs off), accepting 'don't know yet' as an open question.

input: Spec a support agent that answers billing questions and can issue refunds in Stripe. It acts with a service account. Refunds under $50 are fine to automate; larger ones need the support lead. Account deletion and legal threats are out of scope. We have 200 past tickets to test with. Approval requests go to the support lead, who answers within 4 business hours; if they don't, the refund is declined and the ticket is routed to the billing queue. The support lead owns the agent and is the escalation contact. A wrong refund costs money and customer trust; refunds can be reversed only by contacting the customer. Customer emails and payment details are sensitive. We'd pull it if it issues any refund over $50 without approval. The head of support signs off on launch and on raising its autonomy. Anything I haven't covered, treat as don't know yet.
expected_outcome: Recognizes that the prompt already answers the interview questions, so it does not re-ask them, and turns every "don't know yet" into an open question rather than a guess. produces the full agent spec with every section present (purpose, scope, tools and permissions, autonomy levels, approval boundaries, stop rules, escalation, memory, data access, failure modes, must-never-do rules, evals, observability, rollout, open questions). Assigns autonomy per action rather than per agent, writes stop rules with numbers, gives escalations a named owner and timeout, makes each must-never-do rule checkable and covered by an eval case, treats tool output and customer text as untrusted, launches at a lower autonomy level than the target, and closes with open questions, the three riskiest assumptions, and the recommended launch autonomy with the evidence needed to raise it.

input: Our AI ticket summarizer looks great in demos. Help us decide with numbers whether it's ready to ship to all support agents.
expected_outcome: Interviews before writing anything: asks, in one grouped round, what a correct summary looks like for one ticket, who judges correctness, what a wrong summary costs, whether false positives or false negatives are worse, latency needs, the per-request budget, whether real tickets can be used for testing under the data policy, and who can say ship and roll back. Does not write the ship-bar doc, propose thresholds, or invent numbers before those answers, and says the ship bar (success definition, metrics, eval set, thresholds with owners, regression gates, monitoring) comes next.

input: We built an LLM that flags fraudulent refund requests. On 500 labeled cases (60 fraudulent) it flagged 50, of which 45 were actually fraud. One must-pass case failed but the team wants an exception because the rest look good. Are we ready?
expected_outcome: Computes precision on flagged items (45/50 = 90%) and recall against all labeled positives including misses (45/60 = 75%), explains which one to protect for fraud and why, and refuses the exception: a must-pass failure blocks launch with no exceptions. Recommends fixing and re-running, and notes how much one case moves each metric.

input: We shaped a 'shared playlists' feature for our music app: owners invite collaborators by link, collaborators can add and reorder songs. Breadboard it so engineering can slice it.
expected_outcome: Returns the breadboard in the skill's output format: the primary user journey, a UI affordances table, a system responsibilities table, wiring notes connecting affordances to responsibilities, and a slice plan of vertical end-to-end slices that calls out what is fakeable early (stubbed invites, hardcoded data) and splits any slice that grows too big. Does not drift into visual design.

input: Do a competitive analysis for our AI meeting-notes app against Otter, Fireflies, and Granola. We sell to sales teams at mid-market companies.
expected_outcome: Compares competitors on explicit dimensions (core features, pricing model, target customer, UX approach, go-to-market) and for each gives value proposition, positioning, strengths, weaknesses, and gaps versus our product. Ends with differentiation opportunities, positioning options, feature priorities, and underserved segments. Marks competitor facts that need verification instead of inventing pricing or metrics.

input: Our activation rate is stuck at 22%. Plan a design sprint to test a new onboarding flow next week.
expected_outcome: Uses Jake Knapp's five-day structure (Map, Sketch, Decide, Prototype, Test) with the long-term goal and sprint questions, the roles needed (Decider, Facilitator, experts), a realistic prototype scope, and five customer interviews on Friday. Checks whether a sprint is the right tool for this problem and says when it is not.

input: Prioritize these roadmap ideas: public plugin pages, eval dashboards, Slack alerts, usage-based billing, and onboarding docs.
expected_outcome: Uses RICE explicitly: estimates Reach, Impact (on the 0.25-3 scale), Confidence (%), and Effort (person-months) for each item, shows the score calculation (Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort), states assumptions, separates confidence from impact, and recommends a clear next bet while flagging which estimates most change the ranking.

input: Score these with RICE: (1) SSO, requested by 12 enterprise accounts covering 3,000 users a month, about 2 person-months; (2) dark mode, about 8,000 monthly users, 0.5 person-months; (3) CSV export, about 1,500 users a month, 1 person-month.
expected_outcome: Uses the supplied reach and effort numbers, assigns and justifies Impact and Confidence, computes each RICE score correctly, ranks the features, and notes where RICE misses strategic factors (for example enterprise deal value behind SSO) without silently overriding the scores.

input: Our B2B design tool grows mostly through paid ads and CAC keeps rising. Help us design growth loops.
expected_outcome: Distinguishes loops from linear funnels and maps at least one concrete loop (for example user-generated content or a collaboration invite loop) as input, action, output, and how the output re-enters as new input. Names the loop's key metrics and bottleneck, judges fit with the product's existing behavior, and recommends which loop to invest in first.

input: We run a recipe-sharing app. Retention after week 4 is poor. What should our core action and North Star be?
expected_outcome: Applies Sarah Tavel's three levels (grow the core action, retain via accruing benefits, self-perpetuate via mounting loss) to the recipe app, proposes a specific core action and a North Star tied to it, explains what benefit accrues as users do it more, and suggests measurable experiments for each level.

input: We're launching a marketplace connecting local dog walkers with pet owners. How do we solve the chicken-and-egg problem?
expected_outcome: Applies the Hierarchy of Marketplaces: focus on a constrained market (one city or neighborhood) to reach liquidity, decides which side to seed first and how, defines liquidity metrics (for example fill rate and time to match), then covers tipping the market and building defensibility such as disintermediation risk and repeat usage.

input: Design a habit loop for our personal finance app so people check it without push-notification spam.
expected_outcome: Walks through the four phases: Trigger (moving from external to an internal trigger, naming the specific emotion such as uncertainty about money), Action (the simplest behavior done in anticipation of reward), Variable Reward, and Investment (stored value that loads the next trigger). Applies the skill's 'when not to use' boundary: it does not build compulsive loops around decisions users should evaluate consciously (such as trades or large transfers), keeps engagement ethical and in the user's interest, and reduces rather than adds notification dependence.

input: Customers keep churning from our project management tool after 3 months. Help me prep JTBD interviews to find out why.
expected_outcome: Frames churn as customers firing the product and hiring something else, builds a switch-interview guide around the timeline of a real past decision (first thought, passive and active looking, deciding, consuming), and covers the forces behind switching (for example push of the current situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety, and habit). Avoids hypothetical 'would you' questions and names the competing alternatives to probe, including non-consumption.

input: We're about to launch an AI writing assistant for marketing teams. How should we price and package it?
expected_outcome: Applies Monetizing Innovation: puts willingness-to-pay conversations before building or launching, segments customers by needs and willingness to pay, chooses a value metric and pricing model (subscription, usage, or hybrid) with tradeoffs, proposes good-better-best packaging with leaders, fillers, and killers, and lists the WTP research questions to ask. Does not invent market price points as facts.

input: Help my growth team set OKRs for Q1. We want to improve activation and launch a referral program.
expected_outcome: Pushes for focus in the Radical Focus style: recommends one ambitious, qualitative Objective for the quarter (or explains the tradeoff if both themes are kept) with 2-3 measurable, outcome-based Key Results that have baselines and targets, or placeholders where data is missing. Keeps initiatives such as 'launch a referral program' out of the KRs, sets a weekly check-in and quarterly retrospective cadence, and flags pitfalls such as tracking all work as OKRs or spreading effort too thin.

input: Build an opportunity solution tree for increasing 30-day retention in our language-learning app.
expected_outcome: Starts from one measurable desired outcome, maps customer opportunities (needs and pain points phrased from the customer's perspective, not solutions) with sub-opportunities, prioritizes a target opportunity, generates several candidate solutions for it, and designs assumption tests for each. Shows the tree structure and recommends a weekly cadence of interviews and updates.

input: We have 900 active users. How do we measure product-market fit and what do we do with the results?
expected_outcome: Uses the Sean Ellis question ('How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?') with the 40% 'very disappointed' benchmark, defines who to survey (recently active users who experienced the core value), adds the follow-up questions Superhuman used (who benefits most, main benefit, how to improve), and explains Rahul Vohra's method of segmenting to the 'very disappointed' group and building for the 'somewhat disappointed' users who share their main benefit.

input: We built a lightweight CRM, but everyone compares us to Salesforce and we lose. Help us reposition.
expected_outcome: Follows April Dunford's sequence: competitive alternatives (what customers would really do otherwise), unique attributes, the value those attributes enable, the best-fit target customers who care most, and the market category that makes the value obvious. Considers whether to compete in an existing category, a subsegment, or a new one, and avoids generic taglines with no basis in the inputs.

input: Turn this feature idea into a shippable PRD: teams need a way to disable public plugin pages per plugin.
expected_outcome: Uses the PRD-writing skill: problem statement (current situation, pain points, business impact), proposed solution with user stories, goals and non-goals, functional, technical, and design requirements, edge cases, dependencies, rollout, risks and mitigations, and measurable success criteria. Marks assumptions and open questions instead of inventing data.

input: Write a PRD for 'smart reminders'.
expected_outcome: Asks for or clearly marks missing context (users, problem evidence, constraints, success metrics) rather than fabricating it, then produces a PRD skeleton in the skill's structure with explicit placeholders and a short list of the questions that most change the scope.

input: Should our developer analytics tool use freemium or a free trial, and when should sales get involved?
expected_outcome: Applies PLG thinking: compares freemium, free trial, and reverse trial against the product's time to value and the value limits of a free tier, defines activation and the aha moment, defines product-qualified leads with concrete usage signals, and describes a product-led sales handoff. States which data would change the recommendation.

input: We're a B2B payroll startup. Is programmatic SEO worth it for us, and what pages would we build?
expected_outcome: Starts by judging whether SEO fits the business model and search demand before recommending tactics, treats pages as products built for the searcher's intent (for example state-by-state payroll tax calculators or guides with unique data), addresses content quality and indexation risk of thin programmatic pages, covers AI search and answer engines, and defines success beyond traffic (signups or pipeline).

input: One of my senior engineers keeps missing deadlines and it's affecting the team. Help me prepare for the conversation.
expected_outcome: Uses the two axes (care personally, challenge directly) and helps the manager avoid ruinous empathy and obnoxious aggression. Prepares specific, behavior-focused feedback with situation, behavior, and impact, an opening that invites the engineer's view, listening and next steps, and a follow-up plan. Keeps the tone humane and private.

input: We run a vertical SaaS for dental clinics. Which of the 7 Powers could we build, and which are we fooling ourselves about?
expected_outcome: Evaluates each of Hamilton Helmer's powers (scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, process power) for this business, separating the benefit from the barrier for each, rates which are realistic now versus later, calls out powers that do not apply, and recommends where to invest, noting the timing of power in the company's stage.

input: We want to add team-level permissions to our app. Run this the Shape Up way.
expected_outcome: Replaces 'what's the estimate?' with an appetite: decides how much time the work is worth (for example a two-week small batch or a six-week cycle), then shapes a version of team-level permissions that fits it, at a level of abstraction that leaves the team room to design. Names rabbit holes and no-gos, writes a pitch (problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes, no-gos), and explains how the bet works with fixed time and variable scope, including what happens if it doesn't ship within the cycle.

input: Shape a 'bulk edit' feature for our inventory tool before we commit engineering time. We'd give it about two weeks. Goal: warehouse managers can change price, stock level, or category on many items at once instead of one at a time. Non-goals: CSV import and undo history. Constraints: the existing items API, no new database tables, and every change must stay in the audit log. Success: managers stop asking support to run bulk updates for them. I want a Shape Up pitch.
expected_outcome: Runs a shaping session from the boundaries given without re-asking them: keeps the two-week appetite, goal, non-goals, and constraints, defines the problem without jumping to a solution, generates two or three distinct solution shapes, compares them and chooses one, and returns a crisp Shape Up pitch, an open-questions list, and a suggested next step (breadboard, slice, or validate assumptions). Moves anything that does not fit the appetite, including CSV import and undo, to rabbit holes or no-gos and does not invent numbers.

input: Write a stakeholder update for a plugin marketplace launch that shipped public pages, copy buttons, and production onboarding docs.
expected_outcome: Uses a crisp update format: 2-3 sentence summary, shipped work with user benefit, improvements and fixes, metrics only when supplied, risks, asks, and what's next, without overstating unvalidated results.

input: Write a leadership update: the payments migration slipped two weeks because of a vendor API change. Card payments are migrated; ACH is not. We need a decision on whether to delay the price change that depends on it.
expected_outcome: Leads with the slip and the decision needed instead of burying them, states what shipped and what has not, explains the cause and the new date with its confidence, frames the ask with options and their tradeoffs, and stays concise and factual for a leadership audience.

input: Help me rewrite our sales deck. Right now it opens with our feature list. We sell AI code review to engineering leaders.
expected_outcome: Replaces the 'arrogant doctor' pitch (your problem, our solution, why we're better) with Andy Raskin's strategic narrative: opens with an undeniable shift in the world from an old game to a new game, shows how winners play the new game and what is at stake for those who don't, then introduces the product as the way to win (with features as capabilities that get the customer there) and supporting evidence. Keeps the engineering leader, not the company, at the center and drafts the opening slides.

input: We launched a feature that flopped. My boss says it was a bad decision. How do we evaluate that fairly?
expected_outcome: Separates decision quality from outcome quality and names 'resulting', reconstructs what was known at the time and the options considered, assigns rough probabilities to the outcomes, distinguishes luck from skill, and proposes a decision-review habit (for example premortems, decision journals, or a truth-seeking group) for future bets.

input: Our experiment shows a 12% lift in signups, p = 0.04, after we checked results daily and stopped on day 5. Control had 10,000 users and treatment had 9,400 with a 50/50 split. Can we ship?
expected_outcome: Does not accept the result at face value: flags the sample ratio mismatch (10,000 vs 9,400 on a 50/50 split), the peeking and early-stopping problem, and Twyman's law for a surprisingly large lift. Recommends checking the SRM cause, running for the pre-planned duration with a pre-registered OEC and guardrails, and considering an A/A test, then gives a clear ship or no-ship recommendation.

input: Synthesize this feedback: 'Export to CSV keeps timing out' (support, x14); 'I can't find where to invite teammates' (NPS comment, x9); 'Love the new dashboard' (x20); 'Pricing page is confusing about seats' (sales call notes, x6); 'App crashed when uploading a 200MB file' (support, x3).
expected_outcome: Clusters the feedback into themes with counts and sources, assigns severity, prioritizes by impact and frequency (not just volume), suggests solutions, highlights quick wins, and separates praise from problems. Does not invent quotes or counts beyond the supplied data and notes sampling bias across sources.

input: Write an Amazon-style PR/FAQ for a feature that lets freelancers get paid instantly when a client approves an invoice.
expected_outcome: Writes a customer-facing press release in Amazon format (headline, subheading, summary, problem, solution, a quote, how to get started, customer quote) dated to a future launch, followed by external (customer) and internal (stakeholder) FAQs that address cost, risks, fraud, dependencies, and what is out of scope. Keeps the language customer-centric and free of jargon.
